## What the model says

The two-parameter mixture model ([Zhang & Luck, 2008](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature06860)), as
implemented in the R package [bmm](https://venpopov.com/bmm/), describes errors in continuous reproduction with two kinds of trials. On a fraction `p_mem` of the trials the
participant recalls the target, and the response error follows a von Mises distribution (the
circular counterpart of the normal) around 0 with the precision `kappa`. On all other trials the
participant guesses, and every error from −π to π is equally likely. The density of the response
error $x$ is the mixture:

$$
f(x) = p_\text{mem}\,\text{vM}(x;\, \mu = 0,\, \kappa) + \frac{1 - p_\text{mem}}{2\pi}
$$

where $\text{vM}(x;\, \mu, \kappa)$ is the von Mises density with mean direction $\mu$ and precision
$\kappa$. In bmm's model formulas `p_mem` is called `thetat` and is estimated on the logit scale.

`p_mem` sets how much of the distribution sits in the peak and how much in the flat floor, and
`kappa` sets how narrow the peak is. The two do not trade off: changing `kappa` moves no weight, and
changing `p_mem` leaves the width of the peak alone. bmm fixes the location of the memory
component, `mu1` in its formulas, at 0 by default; a systematic bias in the responses can be
estimated by adding `mu1 ~ 1` to the formula.

## The task

One trial is a colour reproduction. The participant sees a display of coloured items, then one item
is cued, and the participant chooses its colour on a wheel. The response error is the angle between
the chosen colour and the target's colour on the wheel, in radians from −π to π. This is all the
model uses of the trial. The colours of the other items, their locations and the set size are not
inputs of the density, which is why the Task settings panel is empty.

## Explore

The Predicted error distribution panel shows the density with the memory component (blue) stacked on
the guessing floor (grey). Move `p_mem` and the blue area grows or shrinks while the floor drops or
rises; move `kappa` and the blue area keeps its size and changes its shape. The bars under it show
the weights, and the readout gives the share of responses within ±20° of the target, the window
shaded in the density panel.

`p_mem` runs over its whole range, 0 to 1. bmm estimates `kappa` on the log scale with a normal(2, 1)
prior; its slider spans the prior mean ± 3 SD and moves evenly in log units, while the number field
shows natural units, from $e^{-1} = 0.37$ to $e^{5} = 148$. The starting values, which the dashed
curve and the "start" bar keep, are `p_mem` = 0.5 (logit 0, the middle of bmm's logistic(0, 1) prior on
the logit scale) and `kappa` = $e^{2} = 7.39$. Typed `kappa` values outside the slider range are used
as long as they are 0 or more. Reset returns both parameters to their starting values.

## In bmm

```{=html}
<div class="ex-widget">
  <pre class="ex-code" id="mix2-code"></pre>
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" id="mix2-copy">Copy</button>
</div>
<script type="module" src="../js/pages/mixture2p.js"></script>
```

The code updates with the controls. `dmixture2p()` returns the density of the response error in
radians. `mixture2p()` defines the model for a data set in which each row is a trial and
`resp_error` holds the response error in radians. The comment in the code gives `thetat`, which is `p_mem` on the logit scale.
`bmf()` writes the formula and `bmm()` estimates the parameters; `my_data` stands for your own data,
and fitting runs Stan through brms. See the
[mixture models article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_mixture_models.html) and the
reference pages for [`mixture2p()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/mixture2p.html) and
[`dmixture2p()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/mixture2p_dist.html).
